overview.body:
**Narasiṃha** ​(*narasimha*) — ‌Man-Lion ‌Avatar · ​The ​Man-Lion — ​the ​fourth avatāra ​of ‌Viṣṇu — ​belongs ​to ‌the Sanskrit ​tradition, ‌where it ​is ‌catalogued under ​the ​domain "Man-Lion ​Avatar". ​The name ​means ‌"The Man-Lion ​— ‌the fourth ​avatāra ‌of Viṣṇu"[^1].

​**Narasiṃha** ‌belongs to ​the ‌Sanskrit tradition, ​where ​it is ‌associated ‌with ‌man-lion avatar.[^2]

​PuniCodex ​restores the ‌name ​as **Narasiṃha** ​and ‌serves its ​temple ​at [narasimha.com](https://punicodex.com/narasimha/). ‌The ​restoration preserves ‌at ​least one ​distinctive ​feature — ​a ‌diacritic or ‌a ​distinctive letter ‌— ​that ​the ASCII ‌form ‌loses, and ‌exactly ‌one historically ​valid ‌Unicode restoration ​exists, ​which places ​the ‌name in ​Tier ​1. The ​plain ‌ASCII form ​*narasimha* ​survives as ​a ‌modern convenience ​imposed ‌by the ​early ‌domain-name ​system; the ‌restoration, ‌not the ​fallback, ​is the ​form ​the project ‌defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

sources.citation: Monier Monier-Williams, A Sanskrit-English Dictionary, Oxford; Cologne Digital Sanskrit Dictionaries, 1899.
Rāmāyaṇa, Vālmīki; translated by Hari Prasad Shastri, 500 BCE.

the-name.body:
The name ​is attested ‌in Devanagari ‌as **नरसिंह**. ​Etymologically it ​means "The ​Man-Lion — ​the fourth ​avatāra of ‌Viṣṇu"[^1].

Sanskrit ​Narasiṃha, from ​nara 'man' + ‌siṃha 'lion'; ​the man-lion ‌avatāra of ​Viṣṇu who ‌slew Hiraṇyakaśipu.

​The ASCII ​form *narasimha* ​survives only ​because the ​early domain-name ‌system could not ​carry diacritics; ‌it is ​a technological ‌compromise, not ​an ancient ‌spelling. The ​Unicode restoration ‌**Narasiṃha** recovers ​the full ​diacritic detail ‌of the scholarly ‌transliteration directly ‌in the ​address bar. ​The restoration ‌preserves at ​least one ​distinctive feature ‌— a ​diacritic or ​a distinctive ‌letter — that ​the ASCII ‌form loses, ​and exactly ​one historically ​valid Unicode ​restoration exists, ‌which places ‌the name ​in Tier ‌1.

The ​letter-by-letter transformation runs:

​- **n** ‌→ **N** ‌— Same, ‌capitalized
- ‌**a** → ​**a** — ‌Same
- ​**r** → ​**r** — ​Same
- ‌**a** → **a** ​— Same
​- **s** ​→ **s** ‌— Same
​- **i** ​→ **i** ​— Same
‌- **m** ​→ **ṃ** ‌— M ​with dot: anusvara
‌- **h** ​→ **h** ‌— Same
‌- **a** ​→ **a** ​— Same

​The canonical ​temple for ‌this name ‌is served ​at **narasimha.com**[^2].

sources.citation: Monier Monier-Williams, A Sanskrit-English Dictionary, Oxford; Cologne Digital Sanskrit Dictionaries, 1899.

pronunciation.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation ‌of ​the ​name is ​**/narasimha/** ​— ​Sanskrit ‌Reconstruction.[^1]

​Phoneme ​by ‌phoneme:

​- ‌**N** ​— Initial ‌character ​of ​the ​restored ​form ​Narasiṃha.
‌- ​**arasiṃha** ‌— Remainder ​of ‌the ​name, ‌preserving ​the ‌distinctive ​marks ​of ‌the ‌Sanskrit tradition.

‌For ​the ​modern ‌speaker, ​the ​closest ‌approximation ​is: ​'NARASIMHA' ‌— pronounce ​the ‌restored ​form ​with ​attention ​to ‌the ‌preserved ​diacritics ‌and length.

​Kindred ​and ‌historical ‌forms ‌of ‌the ​name:

‌- ​**Sanskrit** ​— Narasiṃha, ​the ‌restored ​Unicode ​form ​of ‌the ​name

​Narasiṃha ​is Tier ‌1 ​because ‌the ​Sanskrit ‌form ​preserves ‌distinctive ‌features ​that ​ASCII loses: ​stress, ​length, ‌or ‌special ​characters.

mythology.body:
The ​stories of ‌**Narasiṃha** ‌circulate within ​the ​Sanskrit ​corpus, where ​the ​figure embodies ‌man-lion ​avatar.[^1]

### ​Primary ‌Attestation ​(Sources)

Narasiṃha ‌is ​attested in ‌the ​canonical Sanskrit ​sources ​as ​a figure ​associated ‌with man-lion ​avatar.[^2]

‌### Name ​and ‌Meaning ​(Etymology)

The ‌name ​means "The ‌Man-Lion ​— the ​fourth ‌avatāra ‌of Viṣṇu" ‌and ​reflects the ​figure's ‌role in ​the ​tradition. ‌**Narasiṃha** is ​the ​man-lion avatāra ‌of ​Viṣṇu who ‌destroys ​the demon ​Hiraṇyakaśipu. ​Appearing ​from a ‌pillar ‌at dusk, ​he ‌uses claws ​rather ​than ‌weapons to ‌circumvent ‌the demon's ‌boons ​of invulnerability.[^1] ‌The ​myth ​celebrates divine ​ingenuity ‌and the ​protection ​of the ​devout ‌child ​Prahlāda. The ​image ​of Narasiṃha ‌bursting ​from the ‌pillar ​became ‌a favorite ​iconographic ‌subject, representing ‌the ​omnipresence of ​divine ​protection ​in places ‌where ‌violence is ​forbidden.[^2]
